title: Beyond iReady
author: Annie Karabell, PhD
summary: Guest author Annie Karabell, writing for the parent-advocacy group Schools Beyond Screens, argues that districts pausing or reconsidering iReady contracts are asking the wrong question when they ask 'what would replace it.' She lays out how the platform functions as both assessment and blended-learning tool, and documents specific mechanisms by which it degrades instruction: teachers cannot see the actual questions or student responses behind composite scores, students with entirely different underlying deficits are funneled into identical remedial lessons, and the platform consumes substantial classroom time across three annual testing windows. The piece traces the company's ownership through Curriculum Associates to private-equity firm Berkshire Partners and notes there is no equivalent to an FDA for educational technology products. Karabell reframes the debate away from replacement products and toward the underlying legal and pedagogical requirements schools actually have, pointing to existing clearinghouses for evidence-based instruction as more defensible starting points. The argument culminates in a call for districts to invest instead in differentiated, teacher-led instruction and legitimate multi-tiered support systems rather than a 'sleeker, less infantilizing' successor product.
points: Documents that iReady assigns students with entirely different underlying deficits (e.g., not knowing English measurement vocabulary vs. not being able to interpret graphs) to the identical remedial lesson, exposing the platform's inability to diagnose the actual cause of a low score.

Notes teachers cannot see the specific questions, answers, or strategies behind a student's iReady score, only a composite number, undermining the platform's own stated purpose of informing instructional planning.

Traces iReady's ownership to Curriculum Associates and ultimately private-equity firm Berkshire Partners, framing the product's persistence as partly a market-incentive problem rather than a pedagogical one.

Cites a lawsuit's observation that there is no FDA-equivalent regulator for educational technology, meaning efficacy claims go largely unchecked by any independent authority before reaching classrooms.

Reframes the 'what will replace iReady' question as a false dilemma, redirecting districts toward legally required assessments plus differentiated, teacher-led instruction rather than a newer platformized product.
quotes: Districts spend millions of dollars annually on the assessments and interventions provided through the iReady platform, which is owned by a company called Curriculum Associates, which is owned by private equity firm Berkshire Partners.

Despite these very different learning needs, both students are assigned the same starting lesson: comparing length and height. A human teacher would know that these students need different support and could provide the appropriate instruction with hands-on materials and immediate feedback.

Importantly, teachers cannot see students' assessment results or lessons. These assessments provide educators with only a composite score and a score for each broad domain within a subject area not the questions students answered, their responses, the strategies they employed, or even the time they spent on each item.

As a recent lawsuit noted, 'There is no FDA for educational technology no federal labeling regime, no efficacy review, and no regulator standing between a vendor's marketing and a classroom full of children.'
It is through interaction with responsive, caring, and knowledgeable educators that students gain the social and academic skills to be truly ready for whatever future lives and careers they choose.
